chapters.title: Chapter 5: Reducing Capital Gains Tax Legally

lessons.title: Set-Off and Carry Forward of Capital Losses

body.text: A capital loss is an asset, but only if you use it correctly. Which gains it can offset, the order you apply it in, and whether you file on time can change your tax bill by thousands of rupees.

children.text: Deepak, a 44-year-old dentist in Nagpur, had a mixed year. He booked ₹2,60,000 of long-term gains and ₹60,000 of short-term gains on equity, but also ₹90,000 of short-term losses on shares he gave up on and ₹40,000 of long-term loss on a gold ETF. His broker's report simply netted everything. The Income-tax Act does not work that way, and the order he chooses matters.
The Two Rules That Govern Every Capital Loss

columns.label: Short-Term Capital Loss (STCL)
points: Can be set off against short-term capital gains
Can also be set off against long-term capital gains
The more flexible of the two
Carried forward for 8 tax years if unused

columns.label: Long-Term Capital Loss (LTCL)
points: Can be set off only against long-term capital gains
Cannot touch short-term gains at all
Cannot be set off against salary, business or other income
Carried forward for 8 tax years if unused

markDefs.definition: Moving an unused loss into future tax years so it can be set off against later gains. Capital losses can be carried forward for 8 tax years, but only if the return is filed by the due date.

children.text: Set-off within the same head is governed by section 108 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 70 of the 1961 Act), and
of capital losses by section 111 (section 74 of the 1961 Act). Capital losses can never be set off against salary, business income or interest income, however large they are.

body.title: Which Set-Off Is Allowed?
body.question: Deepak has a long-term capital loss on a gold ETF and short-term capital gains on shares. Can he set one off against the other?
options: Yes, any capital loss can offset any capital gain
No, a long-term loss can only be set off against long-term gains
Yes, but only up to ₹1.25 lakh
Only if both assets are listed
body.explanation: A long-term capital loss can only be set off against long-term capital gains, whatever the asset class. A short-term loss is more flexible and can be set off against both short-term and long-term gains.

children.text: The Order You Choose Changes the Tax

Deepak's short-term loss can go against either kind of gain. His short-term equity gains are taxed at 20%, while his long-term equity gains are taxed at 12.5% and the first ₹1,25,000 of them is exempt anyway. So using the short-term loss against the short-term gains first is worth more.

body.caption: Deepak's year, worked two ways (surcharge and cess ignored)
headers: Plan A: STCL against STCG first
Plan B: STCL against LTCG first

cells: Less: long-term loss on gold ETF

body.label: Cost of the Wrong Order
body.context: Same gains, same losses, same law. Plan A costs ₹8,125 and Plan B costs ₹12,625 before cess, simply because of which gain the short-term loss was applied against first.

body.text: Losses are set off before the ₹1.25 lakh exemption is applied, not after. The exemption works on the net long-term equity gain that survives set-off. That is why using a flexible short-term loss against long-term gains you were not going to be taxed on anyway can waste it.

body.title: Deepak's Tax Under Plan A
body.prompt: Under Plan A, Deepak's taxable long-term gains are ₹65,000 and he has no taxable short-term gains left. What is his total capital gains tax before cess, in rupees?
body.explanation: His ₹90,000 short-term loss wipes out the ₹60,000 of short-term gains completely, leaving ₹30,000 to reduce long-term gains, along with the ₹40,000 gold ETF loss. Long-term gains fall to ₹1,90,000, and after the ₹1,25,000 exemption only ₹65,000 is taxable at 12.5% = ₹8,125.

body.title: The Long-Term Limit
body.textWithBlank: A long-term capital loss can be set off only against ___ capital gains, in the same year or in any of the next eight tax years.
body.explanation: This is the single most important restriction in loss planning. A short-term loss is flexible; a long-term loss is not.

body.title: The Life of a Loss Made in Tax Year 2026-27

events.title: Loss arises and is set off first
events.description: Set-off within capital gains happens in the same year. Only what remains can be carried forward.

events.date: On or before the ITR due date
events.title: File your return on time
events.description: Carry forward is allowed only if the return claiming the loss is filed by the due date. File it even if you have no tax to pay.

events.title: Set off against future gains
events.description: Brought-forward short-term losses go against any capital gains; brought-forward long-term losses only against long-term gains.

events.title: Eighth and final year
events.description: Whatever is still unused after eight tax years lapses permanently.

body.text: A belated return costs you the carry forward. You can still set off losses against gains of the same year in a late return, but any unused balance dies with it. For an investor sitting on a large unused loss, filing a day late can be an expensive mistake.

body.title: Priya Files Late
body.scenario: Priya sold shares in tax year 2026-27 at a ₹3,00,000 short-term loss and had no capital gains that year. Her only income was salary, on which her employer had deducted the right TDS, so she assumed there was nothing to file and submitted a belated return months after the due date.
body.prompt: What did the delay cost her, and what should she have done?
body.modelAnswer: Her ₹3,00,000 short-term capital loss cannot be carried forward, because carry forward requires the return to be filed by the due date. Capital losses can never be set off against salary, so she had nothing to set off against in that year either, and the entire loss is gone. Had she filed on time and reported the loss in the capital gains and carry forward schedules, she could have used it against capital gains for the next eight years. The lesson is to file on time in any year with a capital loss, even when no tax is payable.

body.title: Losses the Law Refuses to Recognise

children.text: Crypto and other virtual digital assets: as Chapter 4, Lesson 4 explained, a loss on one token cannot reduce a gain on another token or anything else, and cannot be carried forward.

Assets whose gains are exempt: if a gain on an asset would be exempt, a loss on it is generally not available either. An original-subscriber Sovereign Gold Bond redeemed at maturity is the clearest example.

Bonus and dividend stripping: if you buy shares or units just before a bonus or dividend record date and sell the originals soon after, the anti-avoidance rules can ignore your loss, adding it to the cost of the bonus units instead. Chapter 2, Lesson 4 covered this.
Personal effects: your car, phone and furniture are not capital assets, so selling them below cost gives no capital loss.

cards.definition: Reducing this year's gains by this year's losses within the capital gains head. Section 108, 2025 Act (old 70).
Moving an unused loss into future years, up to 8 tax years. Section 111, 2025 Act (old 74).
Short-term capital loss. Can offset both short-term and long-term gains.
Long-term capital loss. Can offset long-term gains only.
Apply flexible short-term losses against the most heavily taxed gains first.
File by the ITR due date or lose the right to carry forward the loss.

body.title: Your Loss Housekeeping Routine
steps: Pull tax P&L reports from every broker and a capital gains statement from MF Central before year end
Separate gains and losses into short-term and long-term buckets
Set off losses before applying the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, using short-term losses against the most heavily taxed gains first
Note any brought-forward losses from earlier years and the year each one expires
Report losses in the capital gains and carry forward schedules of ITR-2 or ITR-3, even in a year with no tax payable
File by the due date, every single year in which you have a loss to preserve

points: Short-term capital losses can offset both short-term and long-term gains; long-term losses only offset long-term gains
Capital losses can never be set off against salary, business or interest income
Losses are applied before the ₹1.25 lakh equity exemption, so plan the order of set-off
Applying a short-term loss to 20% short-term gains usually beats applying it to 12.5% long-term gains
Unused capital losses carry forward for 8 tax years, but only if you file by the due date
Crypto losses, losses on exempt assets and losses on personal effects get no relief at all
